The credit-card minimum-payment trap: a smaller bill can hide a longer repayment

Follow the changing payment, remaining debt and interest through four charts comparing a shrinking minimum with a maintained repayment amount.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare a shrinking minimum with a maintained payment

Interactive planning lab

Minimum-only payoff time (months)212

Interest charged in the maintained-payment path$2,668.7

Hypothetical one-balance credit-card model with no new purchases. Interest is opening balance × nominal APR ÷ 12, posted before the payment. The modeled minimum is the greater of the dollar floor and the selected percentage of the balance after interest, capped at the full amount owed. The maintained strategy pays at least the selected amount or the modeled minimum, whichever is higher; the final payment is capped. This is not an issuer calculation, a universal Canadian minimum, or a calculation of Quebec requirements. Actual daily interest, grace periods, fees, purchase dates and payment allocation differ. Each schedule stops at payoff or 600 months. NR means not repaid within that limit, not zero cost. All payments are assumed available and timely. Post-payoff cash is not reinvested.

The central idea

A lower required payment can ease this month’s budget while extending the debt. Track the balance, payoff date and total interest together.

01

Why a shrinking payment deserves a second look

Imagine opening a card statement and seeing that the required payment has fallen. That can be welcome cash-flow relief. It does not tell you how quickly the remaining debt will disappear. When the payment is a percentage of a falling balance, less money may go toward repayment every month, creating a long tail of small payments.

The first chart follows that mechanism. It starts with an existing balance, charges one month of interest and then applies a hypothetical minimum. The comparison preserves a chosen payment amount whenever it exceeds the minimum. Both paths assume no new purchases and payments made on time.

FCAC explains that minimum formulas vary and that paying more can reduce repayment time and interest. Use the agreement for an actual account. The selected percentage and dollar floor here are teaching inputs, not a statement of the rule that applies to every Canadian card.

02

Read the two lines as different household commitments

The maintained strategy is not simply a faster investment return on the same cash flow. It usually requires more money to leave the household earlier. The benefit comes from reducing the balance exposed to future interest; the cost is less cash available for other needs while the larger payments continue.

The payment chart makes that trade-off visible. A chosen CAD 300 amount is treated as a floor, and a higher modeled minimum still takes priority. The final payment is reduced to the amount actually owed. This avoids overpaying the account or treating a selected amount below the minimum as acceptable.

Check that the commitment fits after housing, food, required debt payments and other essential bills. If it does not, a mathematically short payoff schedule has not solved the cash-flow problem. Consider the budget and available assistance before relying on a path that cannot be funded.

03

See exactly what the model calls interest and principal

For an opening balance B and a nominal annual percentage rate a, the simplified monthly interest charge is B × a ÷ 12, with a expressed as a decimal. The amount due becomes B plus that charge. The model then takes the larger of the entered dollar floor and the chosen percentage of that amount, capped at the amount due.

For the maintained strategy, the actual payment is the larger of this modeled minimum and the chosen maintained amount, again capped at the amount due. The new balance is amount due minus actual payment. The following month starts from that balance, so paying principal earlier reduces later interest.

Real cards can use daily calculations and several balance categories. Fees, grace periods, cash advances, promotional terms and payment dates can change results. This example deliberately uses one rate bucket. It does not reproduce a statement, determine a legally required minimum or model the consequences of a missed payment.

04

An unfinished balance is still an obligation

The stacked bars show payments already made alongside the balance still owed at each path’s stopping date. Together they equal the original principal plus the interest charged through that date. If a path has finished, the remaining-balance segment is zero. If it has not, treating payments already made as the full repayment cost would hide debt.

The calculation stops after 600 months. An NR cell means the balance has not been repaid within that window. It does not mean the debt has vanished or that the remaining interest is zero. Low percentage payments at a sufficiently high rate can even allow the balance to grow.

The bars can cover different lengths of time because each path stops when it finishes. They measure nominal cash and debt through those endpoints, without reinvesting payments released after payoff. They are not a comparison of investment wealth at a common future date.

05

Turn the matrix into a payment decision

Read across one rate row to test several maintained amounts. Then read down a payment column to see what a different interest assumption does. The starting balance and minimum rule stay fixed. In every cell, the modeled minimum overrides a smaller maintained amount; the column heading is not a promise that payments never exceed it.

Start with a payment that can be sustained and note its modeled finish date. Next test a modest increase, then a higher rate. If the plan depends on a promotional rate staying low, include the period after it expires using the separate balance-transfer guide.

Review the actual statements as you go. New spending, changed rates and fees can move the endpoint. Once the debt is repaid, make a fresh decision about the cash that becomes available: rebuilding a reserve or funding another goal requires a new instruction, not an assumption hidden inside this calculator.
